title: Body-Fluid Tubes: CSF Order and Synovial Crystals
summary: Send four CSF tubes to the right benches, tell a traumatic tap from true bleeding by watching red cells clear, and keep fake crystals out of joint fluid.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 3 Hits 10 and 12 and Traps 5–6. Adds the traumatic-tap vs bleeding pattern and the acceptability of liquid EDTA. The reviewer’s wording that all three additives form “MSU-like crystals” is softened to “crystal-like artifacts”; its sodium-heparin syringe concentration stays pending.

objectives: Assign CSF tubes 1–3 to chemistry/immunology, microbiology and cell counts, and explain why cells use the last tube.
Distinguish a traumatic tap from bleeding within the CSF using first- and last-tube red-cell counts.
Choose an acceptable anticoagulant for synovial crystal analysis and name those that create artifacts.

scenes.title: Four tubes of spinal fluid
scenes.altText: Four small sterile tubes numbered 1 to 4 fill one after another from a lumbar puncture. The first is pink-tinged; each later tube is clearer. Three lab benches wait: chemistry, microbiology and hematology. Question: which tube goes where?

cues.text: A lumbar puncture collects spinal fluid into four sterile tubes, numbered in the order they fill.
The first tube is pink with a little blood from the needle’s path. Each later tube is clearer.
Chemistry, microbiology and hematology all want fluid. Which tube should each one get — and why does it matter?

scenes.title: One, two, three: chemistry, micro, cells
scenes.altText: Arrows send each numbered CSF tube to a bench: tube 1 → chemistry and immunology; tube 2 → microbiology; tube 3 → cell count and differential; tube 4 → any other tests. A note explains that cell counts use the last tube because any blood from the puncture has had time to clear.

cues.text: Tube 1 goes to chemistry and immunology — tests such as glucose and protein, which a trace of blood or skin from the puncture disturbs least.
Tube 2 goes to microbiology for stains and culture.
Tube 3 goes to hematology for the cell count and differential. By the third tube, any blood picked up by the needle has mostly cleared.
A fourth tube, if collected, is kept for other tests such as cytology or extra studies.
So cells are counted in the clearest tube, where the count best reflects the spinal fluid itself.

props.text: Count cells in the clearest tube

scenes.title: Traumatic tap or bleeding in the brain?
scenes.altText: Two sets of four tubes with red-cell bars. Left (traumatic tap): the red-cell bar shrinks from tube 1 to tube 4 — the blood clears. Right (subarachnoid hemorrhage): the bars stay about the same in every tube. Labels name each pattern.

cues.text: Sometimes the needle nicks a small blood vessel on the way in. That is a traumatic tap, and it adds blood to the first tubes.
In a traumatic tap the blood clears: red cells are high in tube 1 and fall in each later tube.
When bleeding is already inside the spinal fluid — for example a subarachnoid hemorrhage — the blood is mixed through the fluid, so every tube looks about the same.
That is why labs may count red cells in both the first and the last tube and compare them.
Clearing from first to last suggests a traumatic tap. A steady count suggests true bleeding.

props.text: Compare red cells in the first and last tubes

scenes.title: In the lab: synovial fluid and fake crystals
scenes.altText: A joint-fluid sample goes under a microscope. Real needle-shaped crystals appear. Then tubes with oxalate, powdered EDTA and lithium heparin each add look-alike crystal shapes to the field, marked “artifact”. A sodium-heparin tube shows a clean field with a green check; liquid EDTA is also listed as acceptable.

cues.text: Joint fluid is checked for crystals — such as the needle-shaped urate crystals of gout. The lab must be sure every crystal it sees came from the joint.
Some tube additives make their own crystals. Oxalate forms calcium oxalate crystals. Powdered EDTA leaves crystal-like particles.
Lithium heparin can leave crystal-like material too. Any of these can be mistaken for real crystals — a false positive.
Sodium heparin has not been reported to cause crystal artifacts, so it is the preferred additive. Liquid EDTA is also considered acceptable.
The reviewer adds that a syringe can be moistened with sodium heparin before aspiration. Labs should confirm their chosen additive does not mimic crystals.

props.text: Reviewer: moisten the syringe with sodium heparin · labs validate their additive

scenes.title: Two body-fluid traps
scenes.altText: Trap card “CSF tube 1 goes to microbiology because it is freshest” is crossed out → “Tube 1 chemistry, tube 2 microbiology, tube 3 cell count.” Trap card “Any heparin works for crystals” is crossed out → “Sodium heparin, not lithium heparin.”

cues.text: Trap one: “Tube 1 goes to microbiology because it is the freshest.” No — tube 1 goes to chemistry and immunology, tube 2 to microbiology, tube 3 to the cell count.
Trap two: “Any heparin tube works for synovial crystals.” No — lithium heparin can leave crystal-like material. Sodium heparin is the safe choice.
And the clue pair: red cells clearing from tube 1 to tube 3 mean a traumatic tap; steady red cells mean bleeding in the spinal fluid.

props.label: Clearing = traumatic tap · steady = bleeding in CSF

scenes.title: Chem, Bugs, Cells — and Sodium for Synovial
scenes.altText: Memory aid: the numbers 1, 2, 3 above three icons — a flask (chemistry), a magnifier over bugs (microbiology), a cell (count) — with the line “Chem, Bugs, Cells”. Beside it, two S’s link “Sodium heparin” and “Synovial”. A card lists where the aid breaks down.

cues.text: Memory aid for CSF: one, two, three — Chem, Bugs, Cells. Count cells in the clearest, last tube.
For crystals: Sodium for Synovial — two S’s that belong together.

Where it breaks: some labs use five-tube schemes, and when little fluid is collected the lab’s own priority list decides. And liquid EDTA is also acceptable for crystals, so “sodium only” is too strict.

props.label: S + S: Sodium heparin for Synovial

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three numbered tubes labelled Chem, Bugs, Cells, and a sodium-heparin tube beside a synovial sample with a green check.

cues.text: Send CSF tube 1 to chemistry, tube 2 to microbiology and tube 3 to the cell count, comparing first and last tubes to spot a traumatic tap — and collect synovial fluid for crystals in sodium heparin, never oxalate, powdered EDTA or lithium heparin.

explanation.what: Plain language: spinal-fluid tubes are numbered as they fill, and each lab gets a set tube; joint fluid for crystal checks must go in a tube that doesn’t make its own crystals. Scientific terms: CSF tube 1 → chemistry and immunology, tube 2 → microbiology, tube 3 → cell count and differential, tube 4 → other tests. For synovial crystal analysis, sodium heparin (or liquid EDTA) is used; oxalate, powdered EDTA and lithium heparin can produce crystal-like artifacts.
explanation.why: Blood introduced by the needle (a traumatic tap) is greatest in the first tube and clears in later tubes, so cell counts on the last tube best reflect the CSF. Bleeding already within the CSF is evenly mixed, so red cells stay similar across tubes. Additives with crystalline forms can be mistaken for urate or other crystals.
explanation.measure: Labs count red cells in the first and last CSF tubes; clearing suggests a traumatic tap. Synovial fluid is examined by (polarized) microscopy for crystals; anticoagulant artifacts cause false positives.
explanation.differs: Traumatic tap (red cells fall from tube 1 to the last tube) vs subarachnoid hemorrhage (red cells similar in all tubes). Sodium heparin (no reported crystal artifacts) vs lithium heparin, oxalate and powdered EDTA (artifacts).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: which CSF tube for cell counts (3), which for culture (2), the traumatic-tap pattern, the trap that tube 1 goes to microbiology, and which anticoagulant for synovial crystals (sodium heparin).

comparisons.title: Traumatic tap vs bleeding within the CSF

right.label: Bleeding in the CSF (e.g., SAH)
points: Red cells similar in all tubes

comparisons.distinguisher: Whether the red-cell count falls from the first to the last tube.

comparisons.title: Anticoagulants for synovial crystals
comparisons.distinguisher: Whether the additive can leave crystal-like material.

mnemonic.text: 1 · 2 · 3 = Chem · Bugs · Cells — and Sodium for Synovial.
mnemonic.explanation: CSF tubes go to chemistry, microbiology (bugs) and the cell count in that order; synovial crystal samples go in sodium heparin.
mnemonic.limitation: Some laboratories use four- or five-tube schemes, and with little fluid the lab’s own priority list decides. Liquid EDTA is also acceptable for crystals, so “sodium only” is stricter than the evidence.

analogyLimitations: Pink-to-clear tube colours are exaggerated for the cartoon.
Arrow “needles” and question-mark chips are schematic, not real crystal morphology.
Red-cell bars show the pattern, not real counts.
takeaway: Send CSF tube 1 to chemistry, tube 2 to microbiology and tube 3 to the cell count, comparing first and last tubes to spot a traumatic tap — and collect synovial fluid for crystals in sodium heparin, never oxalate, powdered EDTA or lithium heparin.

questions.stem: Three CSF tubes are received, numbered in collection order. Which tube should be used for the cell count and differential?

options.rationale: Correct. The last tube has the least blood from the puncture, so its count best reflects the CSF.
Incorrect. Tube 1 goes to chemistry and immunology; it carries the most blood from a traumatic tap.

options.text: Whichever tube looks clearest, regardless of number
options.rationale: Incorrect. Tubes are assigned by collection number; the last tube is used for counts.

questions.stem: CSF red cell counts are 4,000/µL in tube 1 and 60/µL in tube 4. What does this most suggest?

options.rationale: Correct. Red cells clearing from the first to the last tube indicate blood introduced by the needle.
Incorrect. Bleeding within the CSF gives similar red-cell counts in all tubes.
Incorrect. Meningitis is judged from white cells, glucose, protein and culture, not from red cells clearing.
Incorrect. Clearing across tubes is the expected traumatic-tap pattern, not evidence of mislabeling.

questions.stem: Synovial fluid is collected for crystal analysis. Which additive is most appropriate?

options.rationale: Correct. Sodium heparin has not been reported to cause crystal artifacts and is preferred.
Incorrect. Lithium heparin can leave crystal-like material that may be mistaken for real crystals.
Incorrect. Oxalate forms calcium oxalate crystals — a false positive.
Incorrect. Powdered (crystalline) EDTA can leave crystal-like particles; liquid EDTA is the acceptable form.

claims.text: CSF tubes: #1 chemistry/immunology, #2 microbiology, #3 cell count and differential, #4 other tests.
In a traumatic tap blood clears from the first to the last tube; in a pathologic bleed it is consistent across tubes.
For synovial crystal analysis avoid oxalate, powdered EDTA and lithium heparin; sodium heparin (preferred) and liquid EDTA are acceptable.
Tube 1 is not used for microbiology because it may carry skin contaminants from the puncture.
claims.note: Common teaching; not stated in the sources read.

claims.text: Oxalate, powdered EDTA and lithium heparin form MSU-like crystals; moisten the syringe with sodium heparin (~25 units/mL).
claims.note: Sources describe crystal-like artifacts generally, not specifically MSU-like for all three; the concentration was not verified.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer says all three additives form “MSU-like crystals”; the source read describes crystal-like artifacts without specifying MSU for each.
accuracyFlags.resolution: Lesson uses “crystal-like artifacts” and adds liquid EDTA as acceptable.
